content: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are among the most common bacterial infections in infants and children. Lower urinary tract infections (lower UTIs) are the most frequently encountered type and, in most cases, can be effectively managed with a course of antibiotic therapy, typically without leading to further complications. Various antimicrobial agents have been employed to treat lower UTIs in children, but the specific benefits and potential harms of these treatments remain unclear. The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and harms of antibiotics in the treatment of lower UTIs in children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Renal Group's Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to May 2012. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that investigated antibiotic therapy for bacteriologically confirmed, symptomatic lower UTIs in children aged 0 to 18 years, within primary and community healthcare settings. The data collection and analysis process involved two independent authors who assessed the quality of the studies and extracted relevant data. Statistical analyses were performed using a random-effects model, and the results were expressed as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). A total of 16 RCTs, involving 1,116 children, were included in the review. The findings indicated that conventional 10-day antibiotic therapy significantly increased the likelihood of eradicating persistent bacteriuria compared to single-dose therapy. Specifically, 24% of children who received single-dose therapy had persistent bacteriuria at the end of treatment, compared to only 10% of those who underwent 10-day therapy. The risk ratio for this outcome was 2.01 (95% CI: 1.06 to 3.80), with no observed heterogeneity between studies. However, no significant differences were found between the two treatment groups in terms of persistent symptoms, recurrence of infection after treatment, or re-infection. Additionally, there was insufficient data to evaluate the impact of antibiotics on renal parenchymal damage, patient compliance, the development of antibiotic-resistant organisms, or adverse events. Despite the inclusion of 16 RCTs, the methodological limitations and small sample sizes of the studies made it challenging to determine whether any specific antibiotic or treatment regimen was superior to others. The authors concluded that while antibiotic therapy is effective for treating lower UTIs in children, there is insufficient evidence to identify the optimal type or duration of antibiotic treatment. The review did find that 10-day antibiotic regimens were more effective at eliminating bacteria from the urine compared to single-dose treatments. However, no differences were observed in terms of persistent bacteriuria, recurrence, or re-infection when comparing short-course and long-course antibiotics, particularly when different antibiotics were used in the treatment groups. These findings align with an existing Cochrane review, which also reported no significant differences between shortand long-course treatments when the same antibiotic was used.
